hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? has a thought ever followed you around all day, long after the moment was over?
options: me too. this story is about exactly that.
then you’ll know the monk in this one. listen.
lucky you. keep this one for the day it does.

steps.line: Long ago in Japan, two Zen monks, Tanzan and Ekido, were walking down a country road. The rain had turned it to mud.
At a bend they met a young woman in a silk kimono and sash. She couldn’t cross the mud without ruining it.

steps.q: Monks like these were expected to keep their distance from women. What does Tanzan do?
o: Asks Ekido what they should do
Lifts her up and carries her across
steps.why: He doesn’t stop to debate. He sees someone stuck, and helps.

steps.line: “Come on,” said Tanzan. He lifted her in his arms, carried her over the mud, and set her down on the other side.
Then the monks walked on. Ekido said nothing, all afternoon. But inside, he was turning it over, and over, and over.

steps.q: Buddhist teachers have an old name for a mind that won’t settle, swinging from thought to thought. What is it?
steps.why: Monkey mind, leaping branch to branch. Beginner’s mind and no-mind are real Zen words too, for open and unstuck minds. Ekido’s monkey spent all afternoon on one branch.

steps.line: That night, at a temple, it burst out of him. “Monks don’t go near women! Especially young, lovely ones. Why did you do that?”

o: He apologizes, and promises it won’t happen again
He asks Ekido a quiet question back
He explains that rules can bend when someone needs help
steps.why: He doesn’t defend himself. He turns it back to Ekido, gently.

steps.line: Tanzan smiled. “I left her back there by the road. Are you still carrying her?”

steps.q: Ekido had a real rule in mind. The oldest Buddhist monastic code does bar monks from touching women. What does it hinge on?
o: Any touch, for any reason at all
Touching in public, where people see
Touching with desire in the mind
steps.why: In the oldest code, the rule is about touching a woman “overcome by lust.” Many readers say Tanzan kept the rule’s heart, while Ekido couldn’t stop thinking about her.

steps.line: A sharp comment at nine in the morning can still be riding with you at midnight. Thoughts arrive. You don’t have to carry them.
steps.label: today

steps.q: A sharp comment at nine is still riding with you at midnight. In Zen practice, what’s the first move?
o: Argue it out in your head until it’s settled
Notice it, and name it: thinking
Push it away and think of something nice
steps.why: Many Zen teachers don’t ask you to stop thoughts or win the argument. Noticing loosens the grip, and then the thought can walk on down the road.

say: here’s what i love. tanzan wasn’t careless. he helped, and then he let the moment go. in zen teaching, the trouble isn’t that thoughts come. it’s grabbing on, and carrying them down the road.
so when a thought shows up sounding sure of itself, you can notice it, name it, thinking, and let it pass on down the road. it happens in you. it isn’t all of you.

steps.q: Zen teachers love telling this story to students who keep strict rules. What’s it warning them about?
o: Rules don’t really matter in Zen
You can keep a rule and still miss it
steps.why: Ekido kept his distance, then carried her all day in his head. Tanzan helped, and set her down. The rule was meant to free the mind, not fill it.

today.say: today, when an old moment climbs back on, ask tanzan’s question: am i still carrying this? if you are, name it, thinking, and set it down by the road.
options: good. you might be surprised how light the road gets.
then you know where to set it down. gently.

sources: “Muddy Road,” in Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919), reprinted in Paul Reps, Zen Flesh, Zen Bones (1957): Tanzan and Ekido travel a muddy road in heavy rain; Tanzan carries a girl in a silk kimono and sash across the intersection; that night at a lodging temple Ekido objects that monks do not go near females, especially young and lovely ones; Tanzan answers that he left the girl there, and asks if Ekido is still carrying her.
Tanzan Hara (1819–1892), Japanese Zen monk and scholar.
